$comment: Limitation periods for bringing a compensation claim, by jurisdiction. EVERY entry must be checked by a human (with source) before launch. Entries with verified=false are never shown to users. startsFrom: flight_date = the period runs from the flight date; end_of_year = from 31 December of the year of the flight. confidence: strength of the sources found in October 2026 research (high = official body or supreme court; medium = statute by general rule, secondary sources; low = unsettled or not found). Research is not legal advice: a lawyer should confirm before setting verified=true.

GB-ENG.name: England and Wales
GB-ENG.notes: UK CAA: six years from the incident to go to court in England and Wales (Limitation Act 1980).

GB-SCT.name: Scotland
GB-SCT.notes: UK CAA: five years in Scotland (Prescription and Limitation (Scotland) Act 1973).

GB-NIR.name: Northern Ireland
GB-NIR.notes: Six years under the Limitation (Northern Ireland) Order 1989; found only in secondary sources, not on an official page.

IE.name: Ireland
IE.notes: Six years for contract claims (Statute of Limitations 1957). Official Irish pages don't state the EU261 period explicitly; the 2-year Montreal limit they mention is for damages, not EU261 compensation.

DE.name: Germany
DE.notes: Verbraucherzentrale: regular 3-year period from the end of the year of the flight (BGB §§195, 199); BGH X ZR 62/23 confirms it also for package holidays.

FR.name: France
FR.notes: French government: five years from the incident (Code civil art. 2224), confirmed by Cour de cassation, 10 Oct 2019 (no. 18-20.491). A DGCCRF page still mentions 2 years for delays (Montreal); the Cour de cassation applies 5.

ES.name: Spain
ES.notes: AESA: five years from the flight date to claim from the airline; then one year from that claim to go to AESA's ADR.

IT.name: Italy
IT.notes: Unsettled. Cassazione ord. 4427/2024 excluded the 2-year Montreal period but didn't set one; courts apply 6 months (Codice della navigazione art. 418), 1 year (c.c. art. 2951) or 10 years (c.c. art. 2946). Do not display; tell Italian claimants to act fast.

PT.name: Portugal
PT.notes: No official Portuguese source found. Three years (Código Civil art. 498) is reported in secondary sources only.

NL.name: Netherlands
NL.notes: Unsettled in the sources found: 2 years (Montreal by analogy) vs 5 years (BW art. 3:307). Do not display without legal advice.

BE.name: Belgium
BE.notes: One year for actions under a passenger transport contract (Code de droit économique); the shortest in Europe. A 2022 bill to extend it to 3 years was not found to be adopted. A claim to the airline does not necessarily stop the clock.

AT.name: Austria
AT.notes: Three years (ABGB §1489) per general sources; no OGH decision or official Austrian statement found.

PL.name: Poland
PL.notes: Polish Supreme Court resolution III CZP 111/16 (17 March 2017): EU261 Art. 7 claims prescribe after one year (Kodeks cywilny art. 778).

DK.name: Denmark
DK.notes: Three years under the general Limitation Act (forældelsesloven); only secondary sources found.

SE.name: Sweden
SE.notes: Ten years (Preskriptionslagen 1981:130, applied by ARN). BUT the Supreme Court (NJA 2018 s. 127) requires notifying the airline within a reasonable time; within 2 months of the trip is always in time. Needs a notice warning before display.

NO.name: Norway
NO.notes: Supreme Court HR-2024-1200-A: the Limitation Act (foreldelsesloven) applies, i.e. the general 3-year period (§2), not the Aviation Act.

CH.name: Switzerland
CH.notes: Unknown: no Swiss source on the period (10 years under OR art. 127 is only an assumption). Swiss courts also treat delay compensation differently. Do not display.
